review_notes: I read the whole target file and the lemmas it rewrites with: timeDerivative_mderivClosure_wienerIntegral (DualDerivative.lean), deterministicTimeEmbedding_eq_tensor and predictableProjection_deterministic (ClarkOconeExamples.lean), centeredPartL2_coe and centeredWienerIntegral_coe (NaturalItoRange.lean), and wienerIntegral_wienerIntegralEquiv_symm_apply (TimeDerivative.lean). I grepped the Malliavin directory for uses. The existing simp set here is small and looks consistent (expectationL2_wienerIntegral, centeredPartL2_coe, centeredWienerIntegral_coe, mderivD12_apply). I found no sign of a rewrite loop or competing rules. The findings are about missing canonical rules, not wrong ones. I could not run Lean, so I have not tested that any proposed simp lemma fires or terminates. The main uncertainty is whether the `tensor`-form output of timeDerivative_mderivClosure_wienerIntegral is used elsewhere (outside the directories I searched) in a way that makes changing its statement costly. Adding a new lemma avoids that risk.

findings.problem: timeDerivative_mderivClosure_wienerIntegral gives `tensor g (Lp.const 2 P 1)`. No rule turns that into the normal form that predictableProjection_deterministic consumes. Every use therefore rewrites against the grain with `← deterministicTimeEmbedding_eq_tensor` and then applies `predictableProjection_deterministic`. This three-lemma chain appears at lines 72-74, 91-93 and 169-171 of this file. It appears twice more in ClarkOconeExamples.lean (lines 101-103 and 121-123). A `←` rewrite of a definitional-tensor identity is fragile, and it cannot be used as a simp rule. Neither the derivative lemma nor the surrounding API gives the expression `predictableProjection 𝓅 (timeDerivative … (mderivClosure P (wienerIntegral hB g)))` a canonical form. The `centeredPartL2` and `expectationL2` parts already simplify, but this part does not.
findings.proposed_change: Add a lemma such as `predictableProjection_timeDerivative_mderivClosure_wienerIntegral : predictableProjection 𝓅 (timeDerivative hB L hL hgen (mderivClosure P (wienerIntegral hB g))) = deterministicPredictableEmbedding 𝓅 g`, proved by the existing three-step rewrite, and mark it `@[simp]`. Its left side is the expression that appears in all the first-chaos statements, and its right side is the canonical deterministic embedding, so it terminates. Optionally also add a simp-form variant of timeDerivative_mderivClosure_wienerIntegral that states its right side as `deterministicTimeEmbedding g`, so that tensor does not leak into goals. The five chains can then become `simp` or a single `rw`.
findings.benefit: One canonical simp lemma replaces five copies of an orientation-reversing rewrite chain. Users can reduce a first-chaos Clark–Ocone or duality goal with `simp`. The proofs no longer depend on the order of three rewrites, one of them reversed, so they are less likely to break if `tensor` or `deterministicTimeEmbedding` change.

evidence.excerpt: deterministicTimeEmbedding (P := P) g = tensor g (Lp.const 2 P (1 : ℝ))

findings.problem: The identity `centeredPartL2 (wienerIntegral hB g) = centeredWienerIntegral hB g` is proved inline as a local `have`. It is the only bridge between the two centered-part APIs, and only `centeredPartL2_coe` and `centeredWienerIntegral_coe` are simp lemmas. The bridge uses the simp lemma expectationL2_wienerIntegral, which is declared in this file, so it cannot live in NaturalItoRange.lean unless that lemma moves too. Nothing exposes it to simp. A goal containing `bestNaturalItoIntegrand … (centeredPartL2 (wienerIntegral hB g))` cannot be rewritten into the form that bestNaturalItoIntegrand_centeredWienerIntegral expects.
findings.proposed_change: Promote it to a top-level lemma `centeredPartL2_wienerIntegral : centeredPartL2 (wienerIntegral hB g) = centeredWienerIntegral hB g` (the proof is the existing `Subtype.ext` and `simp only` block) and mark it `@[simp]`. Place it next to `expectationL2_wienerIntegral`. The local `hcentered` then becomes `rw [centeredPartL2_wienerIntegral]` or is absorbed by simp. The orientation is safe: the right side is a strictly more specific constructor and nothing rewrites it back.
findings.benefit: Downstream Clark–Ocone statements can mix `centeredPartL2` and `centeredWienerIntegral` and simplify them to one form. The first-chaos lemma becomes shorter and no longer hides a reusable fact inside a proof.

findings.problem: Three theorems (lines 109-112, 128-131 and 195-198) repeat the same four-line step of rewriting `(Z : RandomL2 P)` into `wienerIntegral hB g` with `g := (wienerIntegralEquiv hB).symm Z`. The source lemma wienerIntegral_wienerIntegralEquiv_symm_apply is not a simp lemma, and it runs in the reverse direction (it simplifies `wienerIntegral (symm Z)` to `Z`). So `rw [hZ]` has to be done by hand. After it, `Z` appears on the right under `g`, so the step cannot be a plain simp rewrite. The file has no `∀ Z, ∃ g, (Z : RandomL2 P) = wienerIntegral hB g` lemma or an induction-style principle.
findings.proposed_change: Add a reusable lemma `firstChaos_exists_wienerIntegral (Z : firstChaos hB) : ∃ g, (Z : RandomL2 P) = wienerIntegral hB g`, or tag wienerIntegral_wienerIntegralEquiv_symm_apply with `@[simp]` (its left side is already in simp-normal form: `wienerIntegral` applied to the `symm` of an equiv). Then use `obtain ⟨g, rfl⟩`-style reduction, or state the `_firstChaos` theorems by `simp`/`rcases` on the new lemma.
findings.benefit: This removes three copies of the same reduction and puts the first-chaos-to-Wiener-integral reduction in one place. Marking the reverse-direction lemma simp would also let simp normalise `wienerIntegral hB ((wienerIntegralEquiv hB).symm Z)` to `Z` in goals.
